paragraphs: The business going forward at present in the pamphlet shops of Paris is incredible. I went to the Palais Royal* to see what new things were published, and to procure a catalogue of all. Every hour produces something new. Thirteen came out to-day, sixteen yesterday, and ninety-two last week. … This spirit of reading political tracts, they say, spreads into the provinces, so that all the presses of France are equally employed. Nineteen-twentieths of these productions are in favour of liberty, and commonly violent against the clergy and nobility; … enquiring for such as had appeared on the other side of the question, to my astonishment I find there are but two or three that have merit enough to be known. Is it not wonderful, that while the press teems with the most levelling and even seditious principles, that if put in execution would overturn the monarchy, nothing in reply appears, and not the least step is taken by the court to restrain this extreme licentiousness of publication. It is easy to conceive the spirit that must thus be raised among the people. But the coffee-houses in the Palais Royal present yet more singular and astonishing spectacles; they are not only crouded within, but other expectant crouds are at the doors and windows, listening a gorge deploye to certain orators, who from chairs or tables harangue each his little audience: the eagerness with which they are heard, and the thunder of applause they receive for every sentiment of more than common hardiness or violence against the present government, cannot easily be imagined. I am all amazement at the ministry permitting such nests and hot-beds of sedition and revolt, which disseminate amongst the people, every hour, principles that by and by must be opposed with vigour, and therefore it seems little short of madness to allow the propagation at present.

paragraphs: You will observe, that, from Magna Charta to the Declaration of Right,* it has been the uniform policy of our Constitution to claim and assert our liberties as an entailed inheritance derived to us from our forefathers, and to be transmitted to our posterity,—as an estate specially belonging to the people of this kingdom, without any reference whatever to any other more general or prior right. … We have an inheritable crown, an inheritable peerage, and a House of Commons and a people inheriting privileges, franchises, and liberties from a long line of ancestors.
… A spirit of innovation is generally the result of a selfish temper and confined views. People will not look forward to posterity, who never look backward to their ancestors. …

Society is, indeed, a contract. … It is a partnership in all science, a partnership in all art, a partnership in every virtue and in all perfection. As the ends of such a partnership cannot be obtained in many generations, it becomes a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.

paragraphs: The English Parliament of 1688 did a certain thing, which, for themselves and their constituents, they had a right to do, and which it appeared right should be done. But, in addition to this right, which they possessed by delegation, they set up another right by assumption, that of binding and controlling posterity to the end of time. …

There never did, there never will, and there never can, exist a Parliament, or any description of men, or any generation of men, in any country, possessed of the right or the power of binding and controlling posterity to the "end of time," or of commanding for ever how the world shall be governed, or who shall govern it … Every age and generation must be as free to act for itself in all cases as the age and generations which preceded it. The vanity and presumption of governing beyond the grave is the most ridiculous and insolent of all tyrannies. … It is the living, and not the dead, that are to be accommodated. …

I am contending for the rights of the living, and against their being willed away and controlled and contracted for by the manuscript assumed authority of the dead, and Mr. Burke is contending for the authority of the dead over the rights and freedom of the living.

paragraphs: Question. What are the duties of Christians toward those who govern them, and what in particular are our duties towards Napoleon I, our emperor?

Answer. Christians owe to the princes who govern them, and we in particular owe to Napoleon I, our emperor, love, respect, obedience, fidelity, military service, and the taxes levied for the preservation and defense of the empire and of his throne. We also owe him fervent prayers for his safety and for the spiritual and temporal prosperity of the state.
Question. Why are we subject to all these duties toward our emperor?

Answer. First, because God, who has created empires and distributes them according to his will, has, by loading our emperor with gifts both in peace and in war, established him as our sovereign and made him the agent of his power and his image upon earth. To honor and serve our emperor is therefore to honor and serve God himself. …
Question. Are there not special motives which should attach us more closely to Napoleon I, our emperor?

Answer. Yes, for it is he whom God has raised up in trying times to reestablish the public worship of the holy religion of our fathers and to be its protector; he has reestablished and preserved public order by his profound and active wisdom; he defends the state by his mighty arm; he has become the anointed of the Lord by the consecration which he has received from the sovereign pontiff, head of the Church universal.
Question. What must we think of those who are wanting in their duties toward our emperor?
Answer. According to the apostle Paul, they are resisting the order established by God himself and render themselves worthy of eternal damnation.

paragraphs: The world desires to be governed by facts and according to justice, not by phrases and theories; the first need of society is to be maintained by strong authority (no authority without real strength deserves the name) and not to govern itself. … The first and greatest concern for the immense majority of every nation is the stability of the laws and their uninterrupted action—never their change. Therefore let the governments govern, let them maintain the foundations of their institutions, both ancient and modern; for if it is at all times dangerous to touch them, it certainly would not now, in the general confusion, be wise to do so.

Let the governments announce this determination to their people, and demonstrate it by facts. Let them reduce the doctrinaires to silence within their States, and show their contempt for them abroad. … Let them be precise and clear in all their words, and not seek by concessions to gain over those parties who aim at the destruction of all power but their own, whom concessions will never gain over, but only further embolden in their pretensions to power. …
Let them maintain religious principles in all their purity, and not allow the faith to be attacked and morality interpreted according to the social contract or the visions of foolish sectarians.
Let them suppress secret societies, that gangrene of society.

In short, let the great monarchs strengthen their union, and prove to the world that while it exists, it is beneficent, and insures the political peace of Europe; that it is powerful only for the maintenance of tranquillity at a time when so many attacks are directed against it; that the principles which they profess are paternal and protective, menacing only the disturbers of public tranquillity.

paragraphs: The principal object then which I proposed to myself in these Poems was to make the incidents of common life interesting by tracing in them, truly though not ostentatiously, the primary laws of our nature … Low and rustic life was generally chosen because in that situation the essential passions of the heart find a better soil in which they can attain their maturity, are less under restraint, and speak a plainer and more emphatic language; … and lastly, because in that situation the passions of men are incorporated with the beautiful and permanent forms of nature. …

For all good poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings; but though this be true, Poems to which any value can be attached, were never produced on any variety of subjects but by a man who being possessed of more than usual organic sensibility had also thought long and deeply. …

For a multitude of causes unknown to former times are now acting with a combined force to blunt the discriminating powers of the mind, and unfitting it for all voluntary exertion to reduce it to a state of almost savage torpor. The most effective of these causes are the great national events which are daily taking place, and the encreasing accumulation of men in cities, where the uniformity of their occupations produces a craving for extraordinary incident which the rapid communication of intelligence hourly gratifies.

paragraphs: … The truth is these wars* group themselves very symmetrically, and the whole period stands out as an age of gigantic rivalry between England and France, a kind of second Hundred Years' War. …

… the explanation of that second Hundred Years' War between England and France which fills the eighteenth century is this, that they were rival candidates for the possession of the New World, and the triple war** which fills the middle of the century is, as it were, the decisive campaign in that great world-struggle. …

But now it is most important to observe further that not only in America, but in Asia also, France and England in that age advanced side by side. … And I find, when I study the English conquest of India, that we were actuated neither by ambition nor yet by mere desire to advance our trade, but that from first to last, that is, from the first efforts of Clive to the time when Lord Wellesley, Lord Minto and Lord Hastings established our authority over the whole vast peninsula, we were actuated by fear of the French.

X8.translation: Text from the first edition (London: Macmillan, 1883); adapted

footnotes.text: Seeley means England's wars with France from 1689 to 1815, which he lists just before this sentence. The first Hundred Years' War was a series of wars between England and France from 1337 to 1453.

By the "triple war," Seeley means a war that began with Spain in 1739 and turned into a war with France, the Seven Years' War (1756–1763), and the war over American independence (1775–1783), which France joined in 1778.

paragraphs: … Mistress now of North America, lording it in India, through the company whose territorial conquests had been ratified by native princes, over twenty millions of inhabitants,—a population larger than that of Great Britain and having a revenue respectable alongside of that of the home government,—England, with yet other rich possessions scattered far and wide over the globe, had ever before her eyes, as a salutary lesson, the severe chastisement which the weakness of Spain had allowed her to inflict upon that huge disjointed empire. …

"For the first time since the Middle Ages," says M. Martin,* speaking of the Seven Years' War, "England had conquered France single-handed almost without allies, France having powerful auxiliaries. She had conquered solely by the superiority of her government."

Yes! but by the superiority of her government using the tremendous weapon of her sea power. This made her rich, and in turn protected the trade by which she had her wealth. With her money she upheld her few auxiliaries, mainly Prussia and Hanover, in their desperate strife. Her power was everywhere that her ships could reach, and there was none to dispute the sea to her. …

The one nation that gained in this war** was that which used the sea in peace to earn its wealth, and ruled it in war by the extent of its navy, by the number of its subjects who lived on the sea or by the sea, and by its numerous bases of operations scattered over the globe. …

paragraphs: The National Assembly, after having heard the report of the ecclesiastical committee, has decreed and do decree the following as constitutional articles:

paragraphs: The French people to the people of ——; brothers and friends:

We have conquered our liberty and we shall maintain it. We offer to bring this inestimable blessing to you, for it has always been rightly ours, and only by a crime have our oppressors robbed us of it. We have driven out your tyrants. Show yourselves free men and we will protect you from their vengeance, their machinations, or their return.

From this moment the French nation proclaims the sovereignty of the people, the suppression of all civil and military authorities which have hitherto governed you and of all the taxes which you bear, under whatever form, the abolition of the tithe, of feudalism, of seigniorial rights and monopolies of every kind, of serfdom, whether real or personal, of hunting and fishing privileges, of the corvée, the salt tax, the tolls and local imposts, and, in general, of all the various kinds of taxes with which you have been loaded by your usurpers; it also proclaims the abolition among you of all noble and ecclesiastical corporations and of all prerogatives and privileges opposed to equality. You are, from this moment, brothers and friends; all are citizens, equal in rights, and all are alike called to govern, to serve, and to defend your country.

paragraphs: Would you have me recognize this liberty, have me fall at her feet, and shed all my blood for her? Then open the prison doors to the two hundred thousand citizens whom you call suspects, for in the Declaration of Rights no prisons for suspicion are provided for, only places of detention. Suspicion has no prison, but only the public accuser; there are no suspects, but only those accused of offenses established by law.

Do not think that such a measure would be fatal to the republic. It would, on the contrary, be the most revolutionary that you have adopted. You would exterminate all your enemies by the guillotine! But was there ever greater madness? Can you possibly destroy one enemy on the scaffold without making ten others among his family and friends? …

I am of a very different opinion from those who claim that it is necessary to leave Terror on the order of the day. I am confident, on the contrary, that liberty will be assured and Europe conquered so soon as you have a Committee of Clemency. This committee will complete the Revolution, for clemency is itself a Revolutionary measure, the most efficient of all when it is wisely dealt out.

paragraphs: Napoleon, emperor of the French and king of Italy, in consideration of the facts: …

5. That this monstrous abuse of the right of blockade has no other aim than to prevent communication among the nations and to raise the commerce and the industry of England upon the ruins of that of the continent. …
We have consequently decreed and do decree that which follows.
Article I. The British Isles are declared to be in a state of blockade.
II. All commerce and all correspondence with the British Isles is forbidden. …

III. Every individual who is an English subject, of whatever state or condition he may be, who shall be discovered in any country occupied by our troops or by those of our allies, shall be made a prisoner of war. …
V. Trade in English goods is prohibited, and all goods belonging to England or coming from her factories or her colonies are declared a lawful prize. …
VII. No vessel coming directly from England or from the English colonies, or which shall have visited these since the publication of the present decree, shall be received in any port.

paragraphs: Spaniards, you have been seduced by perfidious men. They have involved you in a mad conflict and induced you to rush to arms. … In a few months you have been subjected to all the horrors of popular faction. The defeat of your armies was the affair of a few marches. I have entered Madrid. The right of war authorizes me to make a terrible example and to wash out with blood the outrages committed against me and my nation. But my only thought is of clemency. … I will speedily expel from the peninsula that English army which has been dispatched to Spain, not to aid you, but to inspire in you a false confidence and to deceive you. …

Spaniards, your destiny is in my hands. … I have destroyed everything which stands in the way of your prosperity and greatness. I have broken the fetters which hampered the people. I have given you a liberal constitution, and, in the place of an absolute, I have given you a limited and constitutional monarchy. … But if all my efforts should prove useless and if you do not respond to my confidence, nothing will remain for me except to treat you as conquered provinces and to place my brother upon another throne.* …

paragraphs: As far as the German language extended, every one who saw the light within its domain could regard himself as a citizen in a two-fold sense, partly of his natal city, to whose immediate protection he was recommended; and partly of the entire common fatherland of the German nation. …

Let the various conditions among which you must choose pass before you. If you drift along in your torpor and your heedlessness, all the evils of slavery await you—deprivations, humiliations, the scorn and arrogance of the conqueror; you will be pushed about from pillar to post, because you have never found your proper niche, until, through the sacrifice of your nationality and of your language, you slip into some subordinate place where your nation shall sink its identity. If, on the other hand, you rouse yourselves, you will find, first of all, an enduring and honorable existence, and will behold a flourishing generation which promises to you and to the Germans the most glorious and lasting memory. Through the instrumentality of this new generation you will see in spirit the German name exalted to the most glorious among all nations; you will discern in this nation the regenerator and restorer of the world.
P12.attribution: Johann Gottlieb Fichte, German philosopher, Addresses to the German Nation, lectures given in Berlin in 1807–1808
P12.translation: Translated by Louis H. Gray, in The German Classics of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries, vol. 5 (New York, 1914); adapted

paragraphs: In the name of the Most Holy and Indivisible Trinity.

Their Majesties the Emperor of Austria, the King of Prussia, and the Emperor of Russia, having, in consequence of the great events which have marked the course of the three last years in Europe, and especially of the blessings which it has pleased Divine Providence to shower down upon those States which place their confidence and their hope on it alone, acquired the intimate conviction of the necessity of settling the rules to be observed by the Powers, in their reciprocal relations, upon the sublime truths which the Holy Religion of our Saviour teaches:

They solemnly declare that the present Act has no other object than to publish, in the face of the whole world, their fixed resolution, both in the administration of their respective States and in their political relations with every other Government, to take for their sole guide the precepts of that Holy Religion, namely, the precepts of Justice, Christian Charity, and Peace …

Art. I. Conformably to the words of the Holy Scriptures, which command all men to consider each other as brethren, the three contracting Monarchs will remain united by the bonds of a true and indissoluble fraternity, and, considering each other as fellow-countrymen, they will, on all occasions and in all places, lend each other aid and assistance; and, regarding themselves towards their subjects and armies as fathers of families, they will lead them, in the same spirit of fraternity with which they are animated, to protect Religion, Peace, and Justice. …
Art. III. All the Powers who shall choose solemnly to avow the sacred principles which have dictated the present Act … will be received with equal ardor and affection into this Holy Alliance.
P13.attribution: Treaty of the Holy Alliance, signed by Francis I of Austria, Frederick William III of Prussia, and Alexander I of Russia, Paris, September 1815

paragraphs: In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate-street,* where one was reading Luther's preface to the Epistle to the Romans. About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation: and an assurance was given me, that he had taken away my sins, even mine, and saved me from the law of sin and death. …

In the evening I reached Bristol, and met Mr. Whitefield** there. I could scarce reconcile myself at first to this strange way of preaching in the fields, of which he set me an example on Sunday; having been all my life (till very lately) so tenacious of every point relating to decency and order, that I should have thought the saving of souls almost a sin, if it had not been done in a church. …

At four in the afternoon, I submitted to be more vile, and proclaimed in the highways the glad tidings of salvation, speaking from a little eminence in a ground adjoining to the city, to about three thousand people.
P14.attribution: John Wesley, English priest of the Church of England, journal entries for May 24, 1738 (first paragraph), March 31, 1739 (second paragraph), and April 2, 1739 (third paragraph)
P14.translation: Text from The Journal of the Rev. John Wesley, vol. 1 (London: Wesleyan Conference Office, 1903); adapted

paragraphs: Their* object should have been to reconcile to religion, not the sophists, but those whom they were leading astray. They had been seduced by being told that Christianity was the offspring of barbarism, an enemy of the arts and sciences, of reason and refinement; a religion whose only tendency was to encourage bloodshed, to enslave mankind, to diminish their happiness, and to retard the progress of the human understanding.

It was, therefore, necessary to prove that, on the contrary, the Christian religion, of all the religions that ever existed, is the most humane, the most favorable to liberty and to the arts and sciences; that the modern world is indebted to it for every improvement, from agriculture to the abstract sciences—from the hospitals for the reception of the unfortunate to the temples reared by the Michael Angelos and embellished by the Raphaels. It was necessary to prove that nothing is more divine than its morality—nothing more lovely and more sublime than its tenets, its doctrine, and its worship; that it encourages genius, corrects the taste, develops the virtuous passions, imparts energy to the ideas, presents noble images to the writer, and perfect models to the artist … In a word, it was necessary to summon all the charms of the imagination, and all the interests of the heart, to the assistance of that religion against which they had been set in array.
P15.attribution: François-René de Chateaubriand, French writer, The Genius of Christianity, published in Paris in April 1802
P15.translation: Translated by Charles I. White (Philadelphia and Baltimore, 1856); adapted

footnotes.text: "Their" refers to earlier writers who had defended Christianity.

paragraphs: I once heard an orator, in the days when we had political assemblies,* call administrative centralization "that noble conquest of the Revolution which Europe envies us." I am willing to admit that centralization was a noble conquest, and that Europe envies us its possession; but I deny that it was a conquest of the Revolution. It was, on the contrary, a feature of the old regime, and, I may add, the only one which outlived the Revolution, because it was the only one that was suited to the new condition of society created by the Revolution. …

Let no one again express surprise at the wonderful ease with which centralization was re-established in France at the beginning of this century. It had been overthrown by the men of 1789; but its foundations were deep in the minds of its very destroyers, and upon these it was rebuilt anew stronger than ever. …

But when … the bewildered nation began to grope around for a master, immense facilities were offered for the restoration of absolute government; and it was easy for the genius of him who was destined both to continue and to destroy the Revolution to discover them. … Centralization was raised from its tomb and restored to its place; whence it happened that, all the checks which had formerly served to limit its power being destroyed, and not revived, there sprang out of the bosom of a nation which had just overthrown royalty a power more extensive, more detailed, more absolute than any of our monarchs had ever wielded.
P16.attribution: Alexis de Tocqueville, French writer and former government minister, The Old Regime and the Revolution, 1856
P16.translation: Translated by John Bonner (New York: Harper, 1856); adapted

footnotes.text: Tocqueville published this book in 1856, during the Second Empire of Napoleon III, after Louis-Napoleon's coup of 1851.

practice.stem: Mahan's main argument in the passage is that Britain

options.A: won the Seven Years' War mainly because its navy and sea trade gave it wealth and reach
options.B: won the Seven Years' War mainly because its army was larger than the armies of its enemies
options.C: won the Seven Years' War by building a large alliance of European powers against France
options.D: lost much of its overseas trade during the Seven Years' War to stronger French fleets

practice.explanation: Mahan says the one real winner used the sea to grow rich in peace and ruled the sea in war. Trade paid for the war, and the navy protected the trade.

whyNot.B: Mahan credits sea power, not the size of Britain's army. Britain's army was small compared with those of France and Austria.
whyNot.C: Mahan quotes a historian who says Britain won "almost without allies." Its main helpers were Prussia and Hanover.
whyNot.D: Mahan says the opposite: no one could "dispute the sea" with Britain.

practice.hint: Mahan answers the French historian with "Yes! but …" What does he add after "but"?

practice.stem: Which limitation should a historian consider when using this passage as a complete explanation of Britain's victory?

options.A: Mahan quotes a French historian, so his account mainly reflects how the French saw the war.
options.B: Mahan wrote over a century after the war, when few written records from the 1750s and 1760s survived.
options.C: Mahan's naval background may have led him to stress sea power more than other military or diplomatic factors.
options.D: Mahan relies on claims made by Prussia and Hanover, which wanted credit for the victory.

practice.explanation: Mahan's career as a naval officer may help explain why he puts sea power first. To judge why Britain won, a historian should also look at evidence about land war, money, and Britain's allies, such as Prussia.

whyNot.A: Quoting Henri Martin does not make Mahan's account a French view. Mahan answers Martin with his own argument about sea power.
whyNot.B: Many records of the war survived. Historians in 1890 could use printed letters, reports, and earlier histories, and Mahan even quotes Henri Martin's history.
whyNot.D: Mahan does not rely on Prussia or Hanover. He mentions them only as Britain's helpers.

practice.hint: Which choice describes something that is actually true of Mahan or of the passage, and that would also leave the explanation incomplete?

practice.stem: The developments Mahan describes are best understood in the context of

options.A: religious wars between Catholic and Protestant states over the faith of their subjects
options.B: competition among European sea powers for colonies and trade in the Atlantic world and Asia
options.C: efforts by Britain and France to end the Atlantic slave trade in the 1750s
options.D: the spread of factories and steam power across Britain and western Europe

practice.explanation: In the 1700s Britain, France, Spain, and the Dutch Republic competed for colonies and trade. Their rivalry shaped their diplomacy and led to wars fought in Europe, North America, the Caribbean, and India.

whyNot.A: Religious wars mark the 1500s and early 1600s. Mahan's war was fought over trade, colonies, and power.
whyNot.C: Britain did not end its slave trade until 1807, and France later still. In the 1750s both powers were still trading in enslaved Africans.
whyNot.D: Factories and steam power spread mostly after 1780. Mahan's war was fought from 1756 to 1763.

practice.hint: Mahan mentions North America, India, Spain's empire, and bases "scattered over the globe." What were the European powers competing for?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the demands in the cahier?

options.A: The Third Estate wants no tax exemptions and more say in government, under the king.
options.B: The Third Estate wants the Estates-General to replace the king as the maker of France's laws.
options.C: The Third Estate wants the Church's lands sold to pay off the king's debts.
options.D: The Third Estate wants the nobles to keep their offices in return for paying higher taxes.

practice.explanation: The cahier asks that no group be free from taxes, that votes be counted by head, and that offices be open to talent. It also shows loyalty to the king and the Catholic Church.

whyNot.B: Article 8 asks that laws and taxes be ratified by the nation, but the cahier still praises "a beloved monarch" and wants "the stability of the monarchy."
whyNot.C: The cahier does not mention Church lands, and Article 1 asks that Catholic worship be protected. The National Assembly, not this cahier, took over Church lands in November 1789.
whyNot.D: Article 12 asks that offices held by nobles be opened to members of the Third Estate.

practice.hint: Look for what the cahier asks to change and what it wants to keep.

practice.stem: The demand in article 10 is best understood in the context of

options.A: the king's plan to raise new taxes without calling the Estates-General
options.B: a dispute over whether the Estates-General would vote by order or by head
options.C: the nobles' demand that the Third Estate's number of deputies be doubled
options.D: a royal order that the three estates meet in one hall and vote as one body

practice.explanation: If each estate voted as one body, the clergy and nobles could outvote the Third Estate two to one. Counting votes by head would give the Third Estate, with half the deputies, a real chance to win.

whyNot.A: Louis XVI had already agreed to call the Estates-General. The cahiers were written for that meeting.
whyNot.C: In December 1788 Louis XVI's government, on Necker's advice, doubled the Third Estate's deputies. Doubling did not settle whether votes would be counted by order or by head.
whyNot.D: On June 27, 1789, the king told the remaining clergy and nobles to join the National Assembly. This came after the cahiers had been written.

practice.hint: Article 10 talks about how votes "should be taken and counted." Why would the Third Estate care how votes were counted?

practice.stem: Which of the following developments shows the Revolution going furthest beyond the demands in this cahier?

options.A: The National Assembly declared that citizens would pay taxes on an equal basis.
options.B: The Estates-General met in 1789 for the first time since 1614.
options.C: The National Convention abolished the monarchy and declared France a republic in 1792.
options.D: The National Assembly opened government offices to men of talent, whatever their birth.

practice.explanation: In spring 1789 the Third Estate of Carcassonne praised the king and wanted to keep the monarchy. In September 1792 the National Convention abolished the monarchy and set up a republic, going far beyond these demands.

whyNot.A: Equal taxes were exactly what article 11 asked for.
whyNot.B: The meeting of the Estates-General was what the cahier was written for, and article 9 asks for more meetings.
whyNot.D: Opening offices to talent was the goal of article 12.

practice.hint: Three choices match demands in the cahier. Which one does the cahier not ask for?

practice.stem: The decree is best described as an effort to

options.A: make France's clergy independent of both the pope and the government
options.B: strengthen the pope's power to choose and approve French bishops
options.C: put the Catholic Church in France under the control of the state
options.D: return to the Church the lands the National Assembly had taken in 1789

practice.explanation: The decree made bishops and priests elected officials supported by the nation, fit dioceses to the new departments, and required newly elected bishops to swear loyalty. These rules put the Church in France under much greater state control.

whyNot.A: The decree makes the clergy swear loyalty to the nation and takes their pay from the nation. It ties them to the government.
whyNot.B: Article XIX says a new bishop "may not apply to the pope" for approval. The decree cuts the pope's power.
whyNot.D: The decree pays priests salaries from the nation instead. The Church's lands were being sold.

practice.hint: Who chooses the bishops under this decree, and who pays them?

practice.stem: The promise that the clergy "shall be supported by the nation" is best understood in the context of

options.A: the National Assembly's seizure of Church lands to help pay the government's debts
options.B: the pope's offer to pay French priests if the Assembly let him keep naming bishops
options.C: a new tithe that the Assembly ordered French households to pay to their bishops
options.D: the nobles' promise to pay priests' salaries in return for keeping their privileges

practice.explanation: In November 1789 the Assembly put the Church's lands at the nation's disposal, and sales began in 1790 to help with the debt crisis. The state then took on the job of paying the clergy.

whyNot.B: The pope made no such offer. He condemned the decree in 1791.
whyNot.C: The Assembly abolished the tithe in August 1789. It did not create a new one.
whyNot.D: The nobles lost their privileges in August 1789. They made no such deal.

practice.hint: Before 1789, where did the Church get the money to pay its priests? What happened to that money in 1789?

practice.stem: The carrying out of this decree, including a later rule that serving clergy take an oath, contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: strong support for the Revolution among Catholic peasants in western France
options.B: the pope's approval of the election of French bishops by voters
options.C: a drop in the number of nobles leaving France to oppose the Revolution
options.D: a split among the clergy, as many priests refused to swear the required oath

practice.explanation: In November 1790 the Assembly required serving clergy to swear an oath to the new system. About half of the parish priests and nearly all bishops refused. The clergy split, and many Catholics turned against the Revolution.

whyNot.A: Many peasants in the west stood by priests who refused the oath. In 1793 the Vendée region rose in revolt against the Revolution.
whyNot.B: Pope Pius VI condemned the Civil Constitution in 1791.
whyNot.C: More nobles left France after 1790, not fewer, and many priests who refused the oath went into exile too.

practice.hint: Look at Articles XIX and XXI. How would Catholics who stayed loyal to the pope view a Church run this way?

practice.stem: In Source 1, Michelet's main point about the events of October 1789 is that

options.A: the women of Paris wanted to overthrow the monarchy and set up a republic
options.B: deputies of the National Assembly had planned the march to Versailles in advance
options.C: women took the leading part in bringing the king from Versailles to Paris
options.D: the women of Paris marched mainly to punish the queen for her spending

practice.explanation: Michelet compares two great events of 1789: men stormed the Bastille in July, and women brought the king to Paris in October. He gives women the credit for the second.

whyNot.A: The women want the king "amongst them" so they will be "safe from famine." They are not trying to end the monarchy.
whyNot.B: Michelet calls the event "sudden, unforeseen, and truly popular," not planned by deputies.
whyNot.D: Michelet mentions only "some jests" about the queen. The women's concern is bread.

practice.hint: Look at the last sentence of Source 1. What comparison does Michelet make?

practice.stem: The crowd's name for the king, "the baker," most directly reflects

options.A: the belief that a king could cure the sick by touching them
options.B: anger over the high price and short supply of bread in Paris in 1789
options.C: support for the king's plan to sell grain from royal storehouses abroad
options.D: the rise of a new class of factory workers in French cities

practice.explanation: Poor harvests and high bread prices strained many Paris households. The women hoped that bringing the king to Paris would help secure the city's food supply.

whyNot.A: The old belief in the royal touch was about curing disease, not about bread.
whyNot.C: Selling grain abroad would have made bread even scarcer. The crowd wanted grain kept in Paris.
whyNot.D: The march was driven by worries about bread and about the king's response to the Revolution, not by the rise of a large industrial working class.

practice.hint: What are the women carrying, and what do they hope to be "safe from"?

practice.stem: Taken together, the two sources best illustrate which pattern of the years from 1789 to 1804?

options.A: The Civil Code adopted the Catholic Church's rules on marriage and ended divorce in France.
options.B: Women took part in revolutionary politics, but Napoleon's law confirmed men's authority over wives.
options.C: Napoleon's Code copied English law, which let married women manage and sell their own property.
options.D: Women's role in the October march led the National Assembly to fix low bread prices by law in 1789.

practice.explanation: Source 1 stresses women's part in revolutionary action. Source 2 shows that the Civil Code kept husbands' authority in marriage: wives owed obedience and needed their husbands' consent for many property dealings.

whyNot.A: The Code allowed divorce, though it made divorce harder for wives than for husbands. France did not ban divorce until 1816, after Napoleon fell.
whyNot.C: The Code drew on French and Roman law, not English law. English law also gave a husband control of his wife's property.
whyNot.D: The march brought the king to Paris, but the National Assembly passed no such law. Price limits on grain across France came only with the Convention's Maximum laws of 1793.

practice.hint: Compare what women do in Source 1 with what the law allows wives to do in Source 2.

practice.stem: The proclamation in Source 1 was most likely intended to

options.A: assure the rulers of nearby countries that France would not spread its revolution
options.B: persuade the nobles of other countries to give up their privileges on their own
options.C: win the support of common people in lands that French armies had entered
options.D: call on French nobles who had fled abroad to come home and serve the Republic

practice.explanation: The Convention promised to end feudal dues, tithes, and hated taxes wherever French troops went. It hoped ordinary people would welcome the French as liberators.

whyNot.A: The proclamation says France has "driven out your tyrants." It does the opposite of reassuring kings.
whyNot.B: The proclamation itself abolishes privileges. It does not ask nobles to act.
whyNot.D: The Convention treated the émigrés as traitors. A law of October 1792 banished them for life and ordered death for any who returned.

practice.hint: Who is the proclamation addressed to, and what does it promise them?

practice.stem: Policies like those in the two sources contributed most directly to

options.A: the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy in France in 1793
options.B: a long period of peace between France and the Austrian Habsburgs
options.C: the formation of a coalition of European powers, including Britain, against France
options.D: Britain's decision to stay neutral in the wars of the French Revolution

practice.explanation: The promise to overthrow "tyrants" scared Europe's rulers. Then France executed its king in January 1793. Britain, the Dutch Republic, Spain, and others soon joined Austria and Prussia in the war against France.

whyNot.A: The Bourbon monarchy was not restored until 1814. In 1793 the Convention executed Louis XVI.
whyNot.B: France and Austria fought on and off from 1792 until 1815.
whyNot.D: Britain joined the war against France in 1793 and was France's most constant enemy.

practice.hint: Source 2 says France will treat as enemies any people who keep their prince. How would kings react?

practice.stem: The policies in Source 1 are most similar to which later action?

options.A: Napoleon's spread of his Civil Code and legal equality to lands he conquered
options.B: the Congress of Vienna's return of many lands to the families that had ruled them before 1789
options.C: Britain's use of its navy to blockade the ports of France and its allies
options.D: the Holy Alliance's promise that its rulers would govern by Christian principles

practice.explanation: Like the Convention, Napoleon brought revolutionary changes to conquered lands. He ended feudal dues and introduced his Code in places such as the Rhineland and northern Italy.

whyNot.B: Restoring old ruling families did not share the proclamation's goal of replacing privileged institutions, though some Napoleonic reforms survived after 1815.
whyNot.C: A naval blockade was a weapon of war. It did not reform the laws of other lands.
whyNot.D: The Holy Alliance aimed to protect monarchs, not to abolish their privileges.

practice.hint: What does the proclamation abolish, and in whose lands? Look for a later action with the same goal.

practice.stem: The decree was issued mainly in response to

options.A: the king's attempt to flee France and join foreign armies
options.B: foreign invasion and revolts inside France in 1793
options.C: the Prussian invasion that ended with the French victory at Valmy
options.D: Napoleon's call for troops to invade the British Isles

practice.explanation: By the summer of 1793, armies from Austria, Prussia, Britain, Spain, and other states were attacking France. At home, the Vendée and several cities had risen in revolt. The Convention called on the whole nation to fight.

whyNot.A: The king's flight to Varennes was in June 1791, two years earlier. By 1793 the king had been executed.
whyNot.C: Valmy, in September 1792, turned back that invasion almost a year earlier. In 1793 France faced new and larger attacks.
whyNot.D: Napoleon planned to invade Britain in 1803–1805, ten years later.

practice.hint: The decree says it lasts until "the enemy shall have been driven from the soil of the Republic." What was happening in France in 1793?

practice.stem: The decree's call for the aged to "preach the hatred of kings and the unity of the Republic" best illustrates

options.A: the old monarchies' reliance on small professional armies and limited warfare
options.B: a return to the religious motives that had driven Europe's wars in the 1500s
options.C: the Catholic Church's growing influence on the government's war policy
options.D: the use of strong emotion and national loyalty to rally a whole people for war

practice.explanation: The Revolution turned war into a cause for the whole nation. Speeches, songs, and decrees like this one stirred feelings of patriotism and hatred of kings. This showed the emotional power of mass politics and nationalism.

whyNot.A: The decree calls up the whole nation, not a small professional army fighting a limited war.
whyNot.B: The decree asks people to fight for the Republic, not for a religion.
whyNot.C: In 1793 the Revolution was attacking the Church, not following its lead.

practice.hint: The decree gives every age group a job. What is the job of the oldest citizens, and what feelings does it aim to stir?

practice.stem: The decree contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: the collapse of the French army as many soldiers deserted to join the Vendée revolt
options.B: armies large enough to drive back the invaders and then conquer nearby lands
options.C: a decline in France's population that forced the Convention to end the draft in 1794
options.D: an alliance between France and Britain against the Austrian Habsburgs

practice.explanation: The levée en masse gave France the largest armies in Europe. By 1794 French forces had pushed the invaders back, and they soon took the Austrian Netherlands and the left bank of the Rhine.

whyNot.A: The army grew, not collapsed. By 1794 France had about 750,000 men under arms.
whyNot.C: The Convention did not end the draft in 1794. Later French governments kept drafting soldiers.
whyNot.D: Britain and France fought one another through the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, apart from brief periods of peace.

practice.hint: Think about how big an army the decree would create. What could France do with it?

practice.stem: Desmoulins's main argument in the passage is that the government should

options.A: speed up trials so that enemies of the Republic could be punished more quickly
options.B: admit that the Revolution had failed and allow the monarchy to return
options.C: set aside the Declaration of Rights until France had won the war
options.D: release people held on suspicion and show mercy, which would strengthen the Revolution

practice.explanation: Desmoulins wants the suspects set free and a "Committee of Clemency" set up. He thinks mercy, not terror, would make the Republic stronger.

whyNot.A: Desmoulins calls mass executions "madness" and asks that suspects be released. He argues for legal protections and mercy, not faster punishment.
whyNot.B: Desmoulins calls mercy "a Revolutionary measure" that "will complete the Revolution." He does not want a king.
whyNot.C: Desmoulins uses the Declaration of Rights to argue for freeing the suspects.

practice.hint: What does Desmoulins want done with the prisons, and what kind of committee does he ask for?

practice.stem: The "citizens whom you call suspects" had most likely been arrested under

options.A: the Le Chapelier Law of 1791, which banned guilds and workers' associations
options.B: the Concordat, which allowed the government to remove disloyal priests
options.C: a 1793 law letting committees jail people for their views or ties
options.D: the Brunswick Manifesto, which threatened Paris with destruction

practice.explanation: The Law of Suspects of September 1793 let local committees arrest people seen as enemies of the Revolution because of their conduct, words, connections, or social rank. Desmoulins attacks holding people on suspicion instead of for a proven offense.

whyNot.A: The Le Chapelier Law banned workers' groups, but it did not fill the prisons with suspects.
whyNot.B: The Concordat was signed in 1801, long after 1793.
whyNot.D: The Brunswick Manifesto was a threat from Prussia's commander, not a French law.

practice.hint: Desmoulins says there should be no "prisons for suspicion." When did the government begin arresting people because of what they said or who their friends were?

practice.stem: Desmoulins's views in the passage most closely match those of

options.A: Georges Danton and his allies
options.B: Jacques Hébert and his followers
options.C: Saint-Just and the Committee of Public Safety
options.D: Edmund Burke and other British critics

practice.explanation: Danton and Desmoulins were known as the Indulgents because they wanted mercy. Robespierre turned against them, and both were executed in April 1794.

whyNot.B: Hébert's group wanted more arrests and executions, the opposite of Desmoulins.
whyNot.C: Saint-Just, Robespierre's close ally on the Committee of Public Safety, defended the Terror and helped bring Danton and Desmoulins to trial.
whyNot.D: Desmoulins supports the Revolution and the Republic. Burke opposed them.

practice.hint: Desmoulins wants clemency but still supports the Republic. Which group fits both of those views?

practice.stem: Source 1 is best understood in the context of

options.A: Britain's abolition of slavery in its own colonies in the Caribbean
options.B: a massive revolt by enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue
options.C: pressure from British abolitionists, who had already ended Britain's slave trade
options.D: the Declaration of the Rights of Man's clear ban on slavery in 1789

practice.explanation: In 1791 enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose up. To keep the colony and win the rebels to their side, French officials freed the enslaved there in 1793, and the Convention ended slavery in all French colonies in 1794.

whyNot.A: Parliament passed Britain's Slavery Abolition Act in 1833. It took effect in 1834, and forced "apprenticeship" lasted in the Caribbean until 1838.
whyNot.C: Britain did not end its slave trade until 1807, thirteen years after this decree.
whyNot.D: The Declaration of 1789 did not abolish slavery. The assemblies debated slavery and the rights of free people of color before the Convention ended slavery in 1794.

practice.hint: What had been happening in France's richest Caribbean colony since 1791?

practice.stem: Napoleon most likely supported the law in Source 2 in order to

options.A: win the support of free Black leaders in Saint-Domingue
options.B: obey the terms of the Treaty of Amiens, which required the return of slavery
options.C: protect France's plantation colonies by keeping enslaved labor
options.D: reward Toussaint Louverture for keeping Saint-Domingue loyal to France

practice.explanation: Napoleon wanted to protect and rebuild France's colonial economy. The law kept slavery in colonies where the 1794 abolition had not taken effect and allowed the slave trade to supply them, including colonies in the Indian Ocean.

whyNot.A: Bringing back slavery turned free Black leaders against France.
whyNot.B: The treaty returned islands to France, but it did not require France to bring back slavery. That was France's own choice.
whyNot.D: Napoleon sent an army to remove Toussaint. Toussaint was captured in 1802 and died in a French prison.

practice.hint: Source 2 returns the colonies to the rules "in force prior to 1789." What did French colonies produce before 1789, and who did the work?

practice.stem: Napoleon's wider effort to keep or restore colonial slavery, shown in Source 2, contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: the defeat of French forces in Saint-Domingue and the independence of Haiti in 1804
options.B: the end of the French slave trade by order of Napoleon in 1803
options.C: Napoleon's decision to name Toussaint Louverture governor of Saint-Domingue for life
options.D: a successful revolt by enslaved people in Britain's colony of Jamaica in 1803

practice.explanation: The May 1802 law kept slavery in colonies where the 1794 abolition had not taken effect, such as Martinique. French forces also restored slavery in Guadeloupe in 1802. News of that strengthened resistance in Saint-Domingue, where people feared losing their freedom. Fighting and yellow fever destroyed the French army. Napoleon gave up his plans for America and sold Louisiana to the United States in 1803. Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804.

whyNot.B: Source 2 brings the slave trade back. Napoleon did not ban it until 1815, during his brief return to power.
whyNot.C: Toussaint named himself governor for life in 1801. Napoleon rejected this and sent an army against him.
whyNot.D: There was no successful revolt in Jamaica in 1803. Slavery there lasted until the 1830s.

practice.hint: How would people who had been freed in 1794 react to news that slavery was coming back?

practice.stem: The cartoonist most likely intended to suggest that

options.A: Britain and France were ready to share the world peacefully and end their long war
options.B: Britain's navy was too weak to keep Napoleon from taking control of the oceans
options.C: Pitt was defending Britain fairly, while Napoleon alone was greedy for land
options.D: both Britain and France were greedy for power, Britain at sea and France in Europe

practice.explanation: Gillray shows each leader taking the part of the world where his country was strongest: Pitt takes the oceans and Napoleon takes Europe. The title pokes fun at both men's hunger for power.

whyNot.A: The title says the globe is "too small to satisfy such insatiable appetites." Gillray mocks both men's greed, not their peaceful sharing.
whyNot.B: Pitt carves the slice marked "Ocean." The cartoon shows Britain claiming the seas, not losing them.
whyNot.C: Gillray draws both men grabbing big slices, and the title calls both "State Epicures" with "insatiable appetites." He mocks his own prime minister too.

practice.hint: Look at which slice each man is cutting and at the words of the title.

practice.stem: The cartoon is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Congress of Vienna, where the great powers redrew the map of Europe
options.B: the alliance of Britain and France against Russia during the Seven Years' War
options.C: Britain's loss of its thirteen American colonies with French help
options.D: the renewed war between Britain and France after the Peace of Amiens

practice.explanation: Britain and France made peace at Amiens in 1802, but war began again in 1803. In early 1805 Napoleon, now emperor, was planning to invade Britain, and Pitt was building a new coalition against him. In January 1805 Napoleon also wrote to George III offering peace, and the cartoon mocks both sides' appetite for power.

whyNot.A: The Congress of Vienna met in 1814–1815, ten years after this cartoon.
whyNot.B: Britain and France were enemies in the Seven Years' War. Russia fought against Britain's ally, Prussia, for most of that war.
whyNot.C: The American war ended in 1783, more than twenty years before the cartoon.

practice.hint: The cartoon was published in February 1805. What was happening between Britain and France at that time?

practice.stem: Which developments in 1805 most directly support the contrast between British and French power suggested by the cartoon?

options.A: Britain's naval victory at Trafalgar and Napoleon's victory on land at Austerlitz
options.B: Napoleon's landing in southern England after his fleet won control of the English Channel
options.C: Britain's defeat of Napoleon's armies in the long war in Spain and Portugal
options.D: Russia's entry into the war on France's side against Britain

practice.explanation: At Trafalgar in October 1805, the British navy decisively defeated the combined French and Spanish fleet. At Austerlitz in December, Napoleon defeated Austrian and Russian forces. These victories fit the cartoon's contrast between British power at sea and French power on land.

whyNot.B: Napoleon gave up his plan to invade Britain in 1805. His fleet never controlled the Channel.
whyNot.C: The British fought the French in Spain and Portugal from 1808 to 1814, not in 1805.
whyNot.D: In 1805 Russia fought against France. It made peace with Napoleon only in 1807.

practice.hint: Pitt carves the ocean and Napoleon carves Europe. Which events showed each country winning in its own part of the world?

practice.stem: Napoleon's main purpose in issuing the decree was to

options.A: protect the ships of neutral countries from being stopped by the British navy
options.B: weaken Britain by cutting off its trade with the European continent
options.C: prepare the way for a French army to land on the British Isles
options.D: force Britain to hand over its colonies in India and the Caribbean

practice.explanation: Napoleon could not beat Britain at sea, so he tried to ruin its trade. If Britain could not sell its goods in Europe, he hoped it would run short of money and make peace.

whyNot.A: Napoleon complains about Britain's blockade, but Article VII shuts out any ship that has visited Britain, so neutral ships were hurt too.
whyNot.C: The decree aims to cut Britain off economically. Its articles ban trade and shipping; they do not order an invasion.
whyNot.D: The decree targets British trade in Europe. It does not demand Britain's colonies.

practice.hint: Read Articles II, V, and VII. What do they forbid, and whom would that hurt most?

practice.stem: The decree failed to defeat Britain mainly because

options.A: Prussia and Austria refused to join the system and kept their ports open to British ships
options.B: Britain made peace with France in 1807 and won back the right to trade in European ports
options.C: Napoleon canceled the decree in 1808 after French merchants complained that it hurt their own trade
options.D: Britain's navy controlled the seas, and smuggling of British goods was widespread

practice.explanation: Britain kept trading with the rest of the world, including Latin America. On the continent, merchants and even officials smuggled British goods. Smuggling, overseas markets, and uneven enforcement kept the system from forcing Britain to make peace.

whyNot.A: Prussia was forced to close its ports to British goods by the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807, and Austria was also pressed into the system.
whyNot.B: Britain stayed at war with Napoleon from 1803 until 1814. It never made peace to reopen European trade.
whyNot.C: Napoleon tightened the system with new decrees in 1807 and 1810 and kept it until his empire fell. He sold some trading licenses but never canceled the decree.

practice.hint: Check each choice against what actually happened between 1806 and 1814. Did Prussia, Austria, Britain, and Napoleon really act the way the choices say?

practice.stem: The system created by the decree contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: Britain's decision to seek peace with France after its trade with Europe collapsed in 1807
options.B: the end of the Holy Roman Empire and the creation of the Confederation of the Rhine
options.C: Russia's break with the system and Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812
options.D: Spain's request for French troops to defend its coasts against British raids

practice.explanation: Limits on British trade hurt Russia's economy. In late 1810 the tsar relaxed enforcement and let in neutral ships. This dispute raised tensions with Napoleon and helped lead to his invasion of Russia in 1812.

whyNot.A: Britain's trade did not collapse, and Britain stayed at war with Napoleon until 1814 and again in 1815.
whyNot.B: The Holy Roman Empire ended and the Confederation of the Rhine was formed in the summer of 1806, before the Berlin Decree.
whyNot.D: In 1807 Spain let French troops cross its land for a joint invasion of Portugal. Napoleon then widened the occupation and removed Spain's royal family in 1808. Spain never asked France to defend its coasts.

practice.hint: Which large country found that the ban on British trade hurt its own economy? What did Napoleon do about it?

practice.stem: In Source 1, which of the following does Napoleon use as evidence that Spaniards should accept his rule?

options.A: He says he has brought reforms that free the people and limit royal power.
options.B: He claims that Spain's bishops have asked him to protect the Church from the English army.
options.C: He promises to give Spain's colonies in the Americas their independence.
options.D: He promises to return the old Spanish royal family to the throne.

practice.explanation: Napoleon presents his constitution and decrees as proof that his rule will free Spaniards from old restrictions. His claim must be read alongside his threat to treat Spain as conquered land.

whyNot.B: Napoleon does not mention any request from the bishops. In fact, the decrees in Source 2 abolish the Inquisition.
whyNot.C: Napoleon says nothing about the colonies in the passage.
whyNot.D: Napoleon had removed the old royal family. He threatens to treat Spain as "conquered provinces" and put his brother on "another throne."

practice.hint: Look at the second paragraph of Source 1. What does Napoleon say he has already done for Spain?

practice.stem: The decrees in Source 2 are most similar to

options.A: the return of Church lands and privileges under the Concordat of 1801
options.B: the reforms of Spain's Bourbon kings, who relied on the Inquisition
options.C: the Holy Alliance's promise that rulers would govern by Christian principles
options.D: reforms that the National Assembly made in France in 1789–1790

practice.explanation: The National Assembly attacked legal privileges in August 1789 and took over Church lands in November 1789. Some feudal dues had to be bought out until 1793. Napoleon's decrees in Spain likewise attacked inherited privileges and Church institutions.

whyNot.A: The Concordat did not return the Church's lands, which had been sold during the Revolution. Napoleon's Spanish decrees attack old Church privileges, such as the Inquisition.
whyNot.B: Spain's Bourbon kings kept the Inquisition. Napoleon abolished it.
whyNot.C: The Holy Alliance, formed in 1815, defended monarchs and religion. It did not abolish old privileges.

practice.hint: What do feudal rights and the Inquisition have in common? Which earlier government attacked the same kinds of privileges?

practice.stem: Many Spaniards rejected Napoleon's proclamation mainly because they

options.A: saw his reforms as foreign rule forced on them by a conqueror
options.B: preferred the constitution that a Spanish assembly had already written at Cádiz
options.C: expected Russia to send an army to restore Spain's royal family
options.D: hoped to join the Holy Roman Empire under the Austrian Habsburgs

practice.explanation: Many Spaniards, led by priests and local leaders, fought a guerrilla war against the French. They fought for their king, their Church, and their country against a foreign conqueror, even when he offered reforms.

whyNot.B: The Cortes of Cádiz wrote Spain's own liberal constitution in 1812, more than three years after this proclamation.
whyNot.C: In 1808 Russia was Napoleon's ally under the Treaty of Tilsit. It did not go to war with France again until 1812.
whyNot.D: The Holy Roman Empire had ended in 1806, and Spain had never been part of it.

practice.hint: The proclamation is dated December 1808. Check each choice against what had and had not happened in Europe by then.

practice.stem: Fichte's main argument in the passage is that Germans

options.A: form one nation through their shared language and must rouse themselves to stay free
options.B: should accept French rule in exchange for the reforms the French had brought
options.C: should develop a separate language for each German state to protect its freedom
options.D: should rebuild the Holy Roman Empire under the leadership of the Austrian emperor

practice.explanation: Fichte says that wherever German is spoken, people belong to one fatherland. He urges Germans to wake up and resist so that their nation and language will not disappear.

whyNot.B: Fichte warns that if Germans do nothing, "all the evils of slavery" and "the scorn and arrogance of the conqueror" await them.
whyNot.C: Fichte says the German language joins all Germans into one "common fatherland."
whyNot.D: Fichte does not mention Austria or the emperor in the passage. He speaks to the German nation as a whole.

practice.hint: What does Fichte say joins all Germans together, and what does he say will happen if they "drift along"?

practice.stem: Fichte's lectures are best understood in the context of

options.A: the unification of the German states into one empire led by Prussia
options.B: Prussia's defeat by Napoleon and the French occupation of Berlin
options.C: Austria's victory over Napoleon's army at Austerlitz
options.D: Prussia's leadership of the Confederation of the Rhine against France

practice.explanation: Napoleon's forces defeated Prussia at Jena and Auerstedt in 1806 and occupied Berlin. Fichte gave these lectures in the occupied city, urging Germans to see themselves as one nation.

whyNot.A: Germany was unified under Prussia in 1871, long after Fichte.
whyNot.C: Austria lost at Austerlitz in 1805. Napoleon won.
whyNot.D: Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806 as a league of German states under his own protection. Prussia never joined it.

practice.hint: Fichte warns of "the scorn and arrogance of the conqueror." Who was the conqueror, and what had he just done?

practice.stem: Ideas like Fichte's contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: the Congress of Vienna's creation of a single German nation-state in 1815
options.B: Prussia's decision to send troops to help Napoleon invade Russia in 1812
options.C: the spread of Napoleon's Civil Code to Prussia and Austria
options.D: German nationalism in the war of liberation against Napoleon in 1813

practice.explanation: In 1813 Prussia turned against Napoleon, and students and other volunteers joined the fight. They saw it as a war to free the German nation, an idea that writers like Fichte had spread.

whyNot.A: The Congress of Vienna created a loose German Confederation of 39 states, not a nation-state.
whyNot.B: Prussia sent troops in 1812 because Napoleon forced it to, not because of German nationalism.
whyNot.C: Prussia and Austria did not replace their legal systems with Napoleon's Code, and the Code's spread under French rule had nothing to do with Fichte's call for national resistance.

practice.hint: Fichte calls on Germans to "rouse" themselves. What might Germans who took his message to heart do in the years that followed?

practice.stem: The rulers who signed the treaty most likely intended to

options.A: join Europe's Catholic, Protestant, and Orthodox churches under one leader
options.B: create a single Christian empire ruled by the tsar of Russia
options.C: spread the ideas of the French Revolution in a religious form
options.D: base their alliance on Christian principles to help keep order in Europe

practice.explanation: The three rulers promised to act as Christian fathers and to help one another. In practice, the alliance stood for kings, religion, and order, and against revolution.

whyNot.A: The rulers promise to follow Christian "precepts." They do not join the churches together.
whyNot.B: Each ruler keeps his own state. The treaty speaks of "their respective States" and calls the rulers "fellow-countrymen" joined by "fraternity," not one empire.
whyNot.C: The treaty supports kings and cooperation based on religion. It does not proclaim the sovereignty of the people or revolutionary equality.

practice.hint: Who signed the treaty, and what had they just finished fighting against?

practice.stem: The "great events which have marked the course of the three last years in Europe" most likely refers to

options.A: the outbreak of the French Revolution and the fall of the Bastille
options.B: the Peace of Amiens, which ended the war between Britain and France
options.C: Napoleon's defeat and the peace settlement of 1814–1815
options.D: the war between Britain and the United States that ended in 1815

practice.explanation: Between 1812 and 1815, Napoleon's invasion of Russia failed, the allies took Paris, and the Congress of Vienna redrew the map of Europe. The signers saw their victory as a blessing from God.

whyNot.A: The Revolution began in 1789, more than twenty-five years before the treaty.
whyNot.B: The Peace of Amiens was signed in 1802 and broke down in 1803, more than a decade before the treaty. None of the three signers was a party to it.
whyNot.D: That war was fought in North America and at sea, and none of the three signers took part in it. The treaty speaks of events "in Europe."

practice.hint: The treaty was signed in 1815. What happened in Europe from 1812 to 1815?

practice.stem: Which conclusion about cooperation among the monarchs is best supported by the treaty as a historical source?

options.A: It records an acceptance of elected governments, but it does not say who would be allowed to vote.
options.B: It records an agreement to form a joint army, but it does not name the army's permanent commander.
options.C: It records a promise of cooperation, but it does not prove that the rulers kept that promise.
options.D: It records a plan to unite their three states, but it does not give the new state's borders.

practice.explanation: An official treaty is good evidence of what rulers promised. To learn whether they kept those promises, a historian needs other evidence about what they later did.

whyNot.A: The treaty never mentions elections or elected governments. It speaks of rulers who act as "fathers of families."
whyNot.B: The treaty promises "aid and assistance" but sets up no joint army.
whyNot.D: The treaty keeps "their respective States" separate. It joins the rulers in "fraternity," not their lands.

practice.hint: First check each choice against the treaty's actual words. Then ask what kind of evidence a single treaty can and cannot give.

practice.stem: Wesley's account of May 24, 1738, emphasizes

options.A: the value of church ceremonies performed by bishops and priests
options.B: a personal, emotional experience of faith rather than a reasoned argument
options.C: the use of reason to prove God's existence from the order of nature
options.D: his decision to leave the Church of England and start a new church

practice.explanation: Wesley describes a moment of feeling: his heart was "strangely warmed," and he felt sure that God had forgiven him. Methodists stressed this kind of inner experience of faith.

whyNot.A: Wesley's change comes at a small meeting in a house, not during a church ceremony.
whyNot.C: Wesley says nothing about proof. He says he "felt" his "heart strangely warmed."
whyNot.D: Wesley remained a Church of England priest all his life, and this entry does not announce a new church.

practice.hint: Find the words Wesley uses to describe what happened inside him.

practice.stem: Wesley's journal is best understood as part of

options.A: the Catholic Reformation's effort to win English Protestants back to Rome
options.B: deism, which saw God as a creator who does not take part in human affairs
options.C: the Puritan movement that overthrew the English monarchy
options.D: a religious revival that challenged the Enlightenment's stress on reason

practice.explanation: The Methodist revival stressed personal religious experience and the feeling of being saved. This challenged the idea that a religion based mainly on reason was enough, without rejecting reason itself.

whyNot.A: Wesley was a Protestant priest of the Church of England, not a Catholic.
whyNot.B: Deists kept God at a distance. Wesley feels God at work in his own heart.
whyNot.C: The Puritan revolution took place in the 1640s, almost a century before Wesley.

practice.hint: Which words show Wesley treating an inward experience as evidence of his faith?

practice.stem: Wesley's decision to preach outdoors most likely allowed him to

options.A: avoid government officials who had made Methodist meetings illegal
options.B: address large crowds beyond the usual reach of parish services
options.C: follow the orders of bishops who wanted more services held outdoors
options.D: raise money from the crowds to build Methodist churches in the American colonies

practice.explanation: Field preaching brought crowds of thousands, including coal miners and other workers who had little contact with the Church. Methodism grew quickly among working people.

whyNot.A: The passage presents field preaching as a way to reach a large audience. Methodist meetings were not banned, and Wesley was a priest of the official church.
whyNot.C: Many bishops disliked field preaching. Wesley himself first thought it was nearly "a sin."
whyNot.D: Wesley says he "proclaimed … the glad tidings of salvation." He was preaching, not raising money for buildings overseas.

practice.hint: How many people heard Wesley on April 2, 1739? Who might come to hear a preacher outdoors but not inside a church?

practice.stem: Chateaubriand's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: defend Christianity by appealing to beauty, imagination, and feeling
options.B: prove Christianity true mainly by checking the historical accuracy of biblical events
options.C: argue that the Church should give up its political power in France
options.D: call for a return to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy

practice.explanation: Chateaubriand answers Christianity's critics by stressing its kind teachings, its gifts to art and learning, its beauty, and its appeal to the imagination and the heart.

whyNot.B: The passage praises Christianity's cultural and moral effects. It does not test whether biblical events actually happened.
whyNot.C: Chateaubriand does not discuss the Church's political power in the passage.
whyNot.D: Chateaubriand defends the Christian religion itself. He does not mention the Civil Constitution.

practice.hint: Look at the last sentence. What does Chateaubriand want to "summon" to help religion?

practice.stem: The book's publication in 1802 is best understood in the context of

options.A: a revival of religious feeling after the Revolution's attacks on the Church
options.B: the French bishops' public support for the Reign of Terror and its war policies
options.C: the pope's condemnation of Romantic writers as enemies of the faith
options.D: the spread of deism as the official religion of Napoleon's France

practice.explanation: The book came out as Napoleon put the Concordat of 1801 into effect. It belongs to the revival of public Catholic life after the Revolution's attacks on the Church. The Concordat made peace between the French state and the pope and set the Church's place in France.

whyNot.B: The Terror closed churches and attacked priests. The bishops did not support it.
whyNot.C: The pope did not condemn Chateaubriand. The book was welcomed by Catholics.
whyNot.D: Napoleon restored Catholic worship. Robespierre's deist cult had ended in 1794.

practice.hint: What had happened to the Church in France during the 1790s? How might people feel about religion afterward?

practice.stem: The "sophists" whom Chateaubriand criticizes most likely included

options.A: priests who had refused to swear the oath to the Civil Constitution
options.B: Romantic poets who praised nature and strong feeling
options.C: Enlightenment philosophes such as Voltaire who attacked the Church
options.D: Protestant reformers such as Luther and Calvin

practice.explanation: The "sophists" said Christianity was an enemy of reason and learning. Voltaire and other philosophes of the 1700s made this charge.

whyNot.A: Priests who refused the oath stayed loyal to the pope. Chateaubriand would see them as defenders of the faith.
whyNot.B: Chateaubriand shared the Romantics' love of feeling and beauty. He was not attacking them.
whyNot.D: Luther and Calvin were Christians who lived in the 1500s, more than two centuries before this book. They did not call Christianity an enemy of reason.

practice.hint: What did the "sophists" say about Christianity? Which group in the choices would have said that?

practice.stem: Tocqueville's main argument in the passage is that

options.A: the Revolution created a centralized government in France for the first time in its history
options.B: Napoleon restored the local liberties that the Revolution had destroyed
options.C: the provinces of the old regime governed themselves without royal officials
options.D: Napoleon rebuilt the old regime's central government after the Revolution swept away its limits

practice.explanation: Tocqueville says strong central government began under the kings before 1789. The Revolution swept away the things that had held it in check. So Napoleon could rebuild it even stronger.

whyNot.A: Tocqueville says the opposite: centralization was "a feature of the old regime."
whyNot.B: Tocqueville says Napoleon built a power "more absolute than any of our monarchs had ever wielded."
whyNot.C: Tocqueville says centralization was already part of the old regime, so the provinces were run from the center.

practice.hint: Find what Tocqueville will "deny" about centralization. Then see what he says happened to it after the Revolution.

practice.stem: Tocqueville's description of the man "destined both to continue and to destroy the Revolution" best fits which of Napoleon's policies?

options.A: giving back the nobility's tax exemptions while keeping elected local councils
options.B: returning the Church's lands while ending state salaries for priests
options.C: dividing France into self-governing provinces while giving up the title of emperor
options.D: keeping the end of tax privileges while ending free elections and a free press

practice.explanation: Napoleon kept important legal changes from the Revolution, such as the end of inherited tax privileges. But he strengthened his own power and silenced opposition and the press. His Civil Code also kept wives unequal to husbands.

whyNot.A: Napoleon kept equal taxation, and his prefects ran local government instead of elected councils.
whyNot.B: Napoleon did not return the Church's lands, and under the Concordat the state paid priests.
whyNot.C: Napoleon ran France through prefects appointed in Paris, and he crowned himself emperor in 1804.

practice.hint: Tocqueville calls Napoleon the man "destined both to continue and to destroy the Revolution." Find the choice that keeps one part of the Revolution and ends another.

practice.stem: How might the political situation described in the footnote have influenced Tocqueville's interpretation?

options.A: He may have stressed centralization to argue that France needed a more powerful emperor.
options.B: He may have stressed centralization to explain why one-man rule kept returning in France.
options.C: He may have stressed centralization to show that revolutionary assemblies first created it after 1789.
options.D: He may have stressed centralization to argue that France should bring back the absolute monarchy of the old regime.

practice.explanation: Living under a second Napoleon could explain Tocqueville's interest in why strong central power kept coming back. That context helps explain his emphasis. It does not by itself prove or disprove his argument.

whyNot.A: Tocqueville warns that Napoleon's state had a power "more absolute than any of our monarchs had ever wielded." He is not calling for more of it.
whyNot.C: Tocqueville says centralization was "a feature of the old regime," not something the Revolution invented.
whyNot.D: Tocqueville blames the old regime's centralization for making despotism easy. As a liberal, he wanted checks on central power, not a return to absolute kings.

practice.hint: Read the footnote. What kind of government ruled France when Tocqueville wrote, and how might that shape his questions?

exam.title: Unit 5 Practice Exam: Conflict, Crisis, and Reaction in the Late 18th Century
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of European history from c. 1648 to c. 1815. There is no penalty for guessing.
